_note: Quote of the day (/knowledge/quotes). English-language quotations only, in the original wording, by authors who died more than 70 years ago (public domain). Every quote is a line from the author's own work (play, poem, novel, essay, speech, published letter or collected sayings such as Poor Richard's Almanack or Boswell's Life of Johnson) and `source` names that work, with act/scene/chapter where we are sure of it; `year` is the year of first publication or performance. Misattributed classics are left out on purpose (most 'Twain', 'Einstein' and 'Wilde' one-liners, 'Be the change…', 'Insanity is doing the same thing…', Churchill without a source, Sojourner Truth's disputed wording). Verse line breaks are ' / ' (oneLine() in zitateData.js turns them into spaces). `disputed: true` would show an 'umstritten' badge; no quote needs it. `meaning` says the quote in plain English (A2–B1). `words` are the three words a learner needs for it: key `de` holds the English word (key name kept for the code), `art` is a / an / some for nouns (some = uncountable), `pl` the English plural (left out for uncountable nouns), `pos` adj / verb / adv for other words, `hint` an easy English definition, `tr` short glosses (en = short definition, tr, uk, ar, ru, fa). `bio` is easy English, 3–4 sentences. No author has a `bild` (portrait): the pages show initials. The list has 131 quotes, not 366: src/lib/zitate.js repeats the list (day slot modulo list length) when there are fewer quotes than days, so each quote comes up two or three times a year and 29 February shares 28 February's quote. Add quotes only with a documented source; the code needs no particular count. The old `check` URL key is not used any more (nothing reads it).

shakespeare.name: William Shakespeare
shakespeare.bio: Shakespeare wrote about 37 plays and many poems. His plays, such as Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet, are performed all over the world. He worked in London as an actor and writer, and he owned part of a theatre. Many everyday English phrases come from his plays.
shakespeare.kurz: England's most famous playwright. He wrote Hamlet.

austen.name: Jane Austen
austen.bio: Jane Austen wrote six novels about young women, love and money in English country life. Her best-known book is Pride and Prejudice. She lived quietly with her family and never married. Her books were published without her name, and they are still very popular today.
austen.kurz: Novelist of love and manners. She wrote Pride and Prejudice.

dickens.name: Charles Dickens
dickens.bio: Dickens was the most popular English writer of his time. As a boy he worked in a factory because his father was in prison for debt. His stories, such as Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol, show the lives of poor people in Victorian London. He was also famous for reading his books aloud to big audiences.
dickens.kurz: Victorian novelist. He wrote Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol.

wilde.name: Oscar Wilde
wilde.bio: Oscar Wilde was born in Ireland and became famous in London for his witty plays. The Importance of Being Earnest is still one of the funniest comedies in English. He also wrote the novel The Picture of Dorian Gray. In 1895 he was sent to prison, and he died in Paris a few years later.
wilde.kurz: Irish playwright, famous for his wit.

twain.name: Mark Twain
twain.bio: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens. As a young man he worked on Mississippi river boats, and his name comes from a call used on the boats. He wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Many sayings are wrongly given to him, so we only use lines from his books.
twain.kurz: American humorist. He wrote Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.

dickinson.name: Emily Dickinson
dickinson.bio: Emily Dickinson lived almost all her life in her family's house in Amherst. She wrote nearly 1,800 short poems, but only a few were printed while she was alive. After her death her sister found the poems in a drawer. Today she is one of the most important American poets.
dickinson.kurz: American poet of short, deep poems.

franklin.name: Benjamin Franklin
franklin.bio: Franklin was a printer, a writer, a scientist and one of the founders of the United States. He studied electricity and invented the lightning rod. Every year he published Poor Richard's Almanack, a little book full of short, clever sayings. He also helped to write the Declaration of Independence.
franklin.kurz: American founder and inventor. He wrote Poor Richard's Almanack.

lincoln.name: Abraham Lincoln
lincoln.bio: Lincoln grew up in a poor family and taught himself law. He became the 16th President of the United States in 1861. He led the country through the Civil War, and in 1863 he ended slavery in the Confederate states. He was shot in 1865, only days after the war ended.
lincoln.kurz: 16th US President. He led the country in the Civil War.

pope.name: Alexander Pope
pope.bio: Alexander Pope was ill as a child and stayed small all his life, but he became the leading English poet of his time. He wrote long poems in neat rhyming lines, such as An Essay on Criticism. He also translated the Iliad and the Odyssey of Homer. Many of his lines are still used as sayings.

donne.name: John Donne
donne.bio: John Donne wrote love poems when he was young and religious poems when he was older. In 1615 he became a priest, and later he was the head of St Paul's Cathedral in London. His writing is full of strong, surprising pictures. He wrote his famous Meditations while he was very ill.
donne.kurz: Poet and priest. He wrote “No man is an island”.

carroll.name: Lewis Carroll
carroll.bio: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson, who taught mathematics at Oxford. He told a story to a little girl called Alice Liddell, and it became Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. A second book, Through the Looking-Glass, followed. Both books are full of word games and funny logic.
carroll.kurz: Maths teacher who wrote Alice in Wonderland.

stevenson.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
stevenson.bio: Stevenson was a Scottish writer who was often ill and travelled to find a better climate. He wrote the adventure story Treasure Island and the horror story Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. He also wrote travel books and poems for children. He spent his last years on the island of Samoa in the Pacific.

cbronte.name: Charlotte Brontë
cbronte.bio: Charlotte Brontë grew up in a small village in Yorkshire with her sisters Emily and Anne. At first the sisters published under men's names. Her novel Jane Eyre (1847) was a great success. It tells the story of a poor young woman who wants to live as a free person.

ebronte.name: Emily Brontë
ebronte.bio: Emily Brontë was the sister of Charlotte and Anne. She loved the wild moors near her home in Yorkshire. Her only novel, Wuthering Heights (1847), is a dark and powerful love story. She died a year after it was published, at the age of 30.
ebronte.kurz: Author of the novel Wuthering Heights.

eliot.name: George Eliot
eliot.bio: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. She chose a man's name so that critics would take her seriously. Her novels, such as Middlemarch and The Mill on the Floss, show ordinary people in English towns and villages. Many readers think Middlemarch is one of the greatest English novels.

kipling.name: Rudyard Kipling
kipling.bio: Kipling was born in India and wrote many stories and poems about British India. His best-known books are The Jungle Book and Just So Stories. His poem “If—” is one of the most loved poems in English. In 1907 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
kipling.kurz: Born in India. He wrote The Jungle Book and the poem “If—”.

yeats.name: W. B. Yeats
yeats.bio: William Butler Yeats was the most important Irish poet of his time. His early poems are about Irish legends and dreams, and his later poems are about politics and growing old. He helped to start the Abbey Theatre in Dublin. In 1923 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
yeats.kurz: Irish poet and Nobel Prize winner.

woolf.name: Virginia Woolf
woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was part of the Bloomsbury Group, a circle of writers and artists in London. In novels such as Mrs Dalloway she wrote about the thoughts of her characters in a new way. Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) is about women and writing. She and her husband also ran a small publishing house, the Hogarth Press.
woolf.kurz: Novelist and essayist. She wrote Mrs Dalloway.

whitman.name: Walt Whitman
whitman.bio: Walt Whitman worked as a printer, a teacher and a journalist. His book of poems Leaves of Grass, which he rewrote for most of his life, changed American poetry. He used free verse, without rhyme, and wrote about ordinary people. During the Civil War he helped to care for wounded soldiers.
whitman.kurz: American poet of Leaves of Grass.

thoreau.name: Henry David Thoreau
thoreau.bio: Thoreau lived for two years in a small cabin by Walden Pond in Massachusetts. He wrote about this simple life in his book Walden. He also wrote an essay about refusing to obey unjust laws, which later inspired Gandhi and Martin Luther King. He loved nature and kept a diary of the plants and animals he saw.
thoreau.kurz: American writer. He lived in a cabin and wrote Walden.

emerson.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
emerson.bio: Emerson was a minister who left the church to become a writer and speaker. He travelled around the United States and gave lectures to big audiences. In essays such as Self-Reliance he asked people to trust their own thinking. He was a friend and teacher of Thoreau.

poe.name: Edgar Allan Poe
poe.bio: Poe lost his parents very young and lived a hard, poor life. He wrote dark poems and scary stories, such as The Raven and The Tell-Tale Heart. He also wrote some of the first detective stories. He died in Baltimore at the age of 40.
poe.kurz: American author of dark poems and scary stories.

burns.name: Robert Burns
burns.bio: Robert Burns was the son of a poor farmer in Scotland and worked on the land himself. He wrote poems and songs in Scots and in English. His song “Auld Lang Syne” is sung on New Year's Eve all over the world. Scots celebrate his birthday on 25 January with Burns Night.

wordsworth.name: William Wordsworth
wordsworth.bio: Wordsworth loved the Lake District in the north of England and wrote about its hills and lakes. With his friend Coleridge he published Lyrical Ballads (1798), a book that started the Romantic movement. He wanted poems to use simple, everyday language. In 1843 he became Poet Laureate.
wordsworth.kurz: Romantic poet of nature. He wrote “Daffodils”.

keats.name: John Keats
keats.bio: John Keats trained as a doctor but chose to be a poet. He wrote his best poems, the great odes, in only a few years. He became ill with tuberculosis and died in Rome at the age of 25. Only after his death did he become famous.

pshelley.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
pshelley.bio: Percy Shelley was a Romantic poet with strong political ideas. He was sent away from Oxford University for writing about atheism. He lived in Italy for his last years and drowned in a boat accident at the age of 29. His wife was the writer Mary Shelley.

byron.name: Lord Byron
byron.bio: George Gordon, Lord Byron, was a famous and much-discussed poet. He travelled through Europe and wrote long poems about his journeys, such as Don Juan. He loved Greece and went there to fight for its freedom. He died in Greece at the age of 36.
byron.kurz: Romantic poet, famous for his adventurous life.

johnson.name: Samuel Johnson
johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was a poor student who became the most respected writer of his time in London. He wrote the Dictionary of the English Language (1755) almost alone, and it took him nine years. He was known for his sharp, funny conversation. His friend James Boswell wrote down many of his sayings in The Life of Samuel Johnson.
johnson.kurz: He wrote the first great English dictionary.

mshelley.name: Mary Shelley
mshelley.bio: Mary Shelley was the daughter of two famous writers, Mary Wollstonecraft and William Godwin. She began her novel Frankenstein when she was 18, during a rainy summer in Switzerland. The book is about a scientist who makes a living creature. It is often called the first science-fiction novel.
mshelley.kurz: She wrote Frankenstein at the age of 18.

melville.name: Herman Melville
melville.bio: Herman Melville worked on whaling ships as a young man. He used these experiences in his great novel Moby-Dick (1851), about Captain Ahab and a white whale. The book sold badly, and he later worked as a customs officer. Only after his death did readers see how important it is.

douglass.name: Frederick Douglass
douglass.bio: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery and escaped in 1838. He taught himself to read and write. He became a leading speaker against slavery and wrote the book Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass. Later he worked for equal rights for black people and for women.
douglass.kurz: Escaped slave who became a great speaker.

doyle.name: Arthur Conan Doyle
doyle.bio: Arthur Conan Doyle was a doctor in Scotland and England. In 1887 he invented the detective Sherlock Holmes and his friend Dr Watson. He wrote four novels and 56 short stories about them. Holmes became so famous that many people thought he was real.

milton.name: John Milton
milton.bio: John Milton wrote poems, essays and political texts. He worked for the government during the English Civil War. He went blind in his forties, but he went on writing by telling his words to helpers. His long poem Paradise Lost (1667) is one of the great works in English.
milton.kurz: He wrote Paradise Lost, even though he was blind.

tennyson.name: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
tennyson.bio: Tennyson was the favourite poet of Queen Victoria and became Poet Laureate in 1850. He wrote poems about the legend of King Arthur and about brave soldiers. His long poem In Memoriam is about the death of his close friend. Many of his lines are known by heart in Britain.

rbrowning.name: Robert Browning
rbrowning.bio: Robert Browning wrote poems in the voices of different people, such as a painter or a duke. In 1846 he secretly married the poet Elizabeth Barrett and moved with her to Italy. They lived there happily for many years. His poems are known for their strong characters.

ebbrowning.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
ebbrowning.bio: Elizabeth Barrett was often ill and spent years in her room in London. She wrote poems that Robert Browning loved, and he wrote to her. They married in secret and moved to Italy. Her Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850) are love poems to her husband.

blake.name: William Blake
blake.bio: William Blake lived and worked in London as an engraver. He wrote his poems and drew the pictures for them himself. He said he saw angels and visions. Almost nobody bought his books while he was alive, but today he is one of the best-loved English poets.
blake.kurz: Poet and artist. He wrote “The Tyger”.

coleridge.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
coleridge.bio: Coleridge was a close friend of Wordsworth, and together they published Lyrical Ballads. His long poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner tells of a sailor who shoots a bird and is punished by the sea. He also wrote “Kubla Khan”, which he said came to him in a dream. In later life he gave lectures about Shakespeare and philosophy.
coleridge.kurz: Poet of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

bacon.name: Francis Bacon
bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was a lawyer and a high official under Queen Elizabeth I and King James I. He also wrote about science and said that people should learn from experiments. His short Essays (1625) are full of clear advice. Many of his sentences are still quoted today.

fitzgerald.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
fitzgerald.bio: Fitzgerald became famous at 24 with his first novel. He wrote about rich, young Americans in the 1920s, the Jazz Age. His best-known book, The Great Gatsby (1925), sold badly at first but is now seen as a classic. He worked as a writer in Hollywood in his last years and died at 44.

fdr.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
fdr.bio: Roosevelt was the 32nd President of the United States and was elected four times. He led the country out of the Great Depression and through most of the Second World War. He could not walk without help after an illness at the age of 39. He talked to the people on the radio in his “fireside chats”.
fdr.kurz: US President in the Great Depression and the war.

wollstonecraft.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
wollstonecraft.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft worked as a teacher, a governess and a writer. In 1792 she published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, in which she asked for good schools for girls. She is seen as one of the first women to argue for equal rights. She died after the birth of her daughter, the future author Mary Shelley.

lear.name: Edward Lear
lear.bio: Edward Lear painted birds and landscapes and travelled a lot, but he is best known for his nonsense poems. He wrote funny verses and drew silly pictures for them. “The Owl and the Pussy-cat” is his most famous poem. Children in England still learn it today.
